name: Hoboken Terminal and its yard (Delaware, Lackawanna & Western)
note: The first terminal opened 14 November 1862 (Morris and Essex Railroad), the second 15 January 1868, the fourth in 1885; "the rail and ferry terminal buildings were constructed in 1907". The yard and slips stand in the cove between Hoboken and Jersey City. Start year estimated (two years before the first terminal). Ring = the Overture outline of the terminal and yard + 40 m.

name: Paulus Hook: the island, the marsh behind it and the fill out to the pier line (Columbus Drive to the Morris Canal basin)
note: "The first settlement at Paulus Hook was in 1633 when the area was an island at high tide." The Associates of the Jersey Company, chartered 10 November 1804, laid out the town on it; rail service to the Hook began in 1834 and the Pennsylvania Railroad rebuilt its Exchange Place terminal in 1876 and 1888-1892. Start = the charter; end = the last terminal: both ends are stated events, the progress between them is estimated (estimated bracket: no source dates the fill itself). Ring = today's land east of Marin Boulevard (Henderson St) and south of Columbus Drive; it contains the natural island.

name: Harsimus Cove, the first quarter mile east of Henderson Street (Marin Boulevard), Columbus Drive to 6th Street
note: "By 1870 much of the estuary flood zone was land-filled for the development of railyards, extending a quarter mile from Henderson Street." Ring = 402 m (a quarter mile) east of Marin Boulevard. Start year estimated.

name: Harsimus Cove beyond the first quarter mile: the Pennsylvania Railroad's Harsimus Yards
note: The landfilling of the remainder of Harsimus Cove "in the early 1870s" created the Harsimus Yards of the Pennsylvania Railroad (Jersey City Landmarks Conservancy, Warehouse Historic District); the Pennsylvania took over the line in 1871. End year estimated from "early 1870s". Ring = today's land more than a quarter mile east of Marin Boulevard, Columbus Drive to 6th Street; piers of later date are inside.

name: Pavonia: the Long Dock Company's fill for the Erie terminal (6th Street to the Hoboken line)
note: The Erie reached the river through the Long Dock Tunnel, "started in 1856 and opened in 1861"; its Pavonia Terminal, "built on the northern portion of landfilled Harsimus Cove", "opened in 1861". Both years documented for the works; piers and yard extensions of later years are inside the ring and not dated separately. Ring = today's land east of Marin Boulevard from 6th Street to the city line (Newport).

name: Downtown Jersey City west of Henderson Street: the salt meadow between Harsimus and Bergen Hill
note: Harsimus was upland in a tidal marsh ("Crow's Marsh"); Van Vorst Township, laid out on it, was annexed by Jersey City in 1851. No source dates the filling of the meadow: estimated bracket. Ring = 1 km west of Marin Boulevard from Grand Street to the city line; it contains the Harsimus upland and the foot of Bergen Hill.

name: South Cove: the Morris Canal basins and Liberty Harbor (Grand Street to the Tidewater Basin)
note: The Morris Canal was "extended eastward to Jersey City between 1834 and 1836" and ended in basins in South Cove; the Lehigh Valley leased the canal "which includes the canal basin at South Cove" in 1871. Liberty Harbor "consists primarily of landfill"; "tidal creeks, marshes, and shallow coves - portions of which were later filled". Start = the canal; end year estimated (estimated bracket). Ring = today's land south of Grand Street, up to 1 km west of Marin Boulevard.

name: Hoboken: the island round Castle Point, the Hoboken Meadows west of it and the river front
note: "In the 1700s, Hoboken was an island"; "the island, the elevated area around Castle Point, comprised about 25 percent of Hoboken's current land mass. The remainder of Hoboken was a wetland, a salt marsh - The Hoboken Meadows"; "continued dumping of fill into the Hoboken Meadows allowed the city to eventually expand west to the Palisades and north to 16th Street" (Fund for a Better Waterfront on the Hoboken Historical Museum's exhibition). "In the 1820s, the Stevens family began to drain the swamp and fill nearby marshes" (Wikipedia, Elysian Fields). Start = 1820s; end year estimated (the west side was built up at the turn of the 20th century). Ring = the whole city on today's land; the natural island is inside.

name: Communipaw Cove: the Central Railroad of New Jersey terminal and yards (Liberty State Park, north and middle)
note: New Jersey DEP, park history: the Central Railroad of New Jersey "purchased and began filling Communipaw Cove. Between 1860 and 1928, as the need to expand their facility grew, they continued filling the cove" (read through a search-result summary on 2026-11-10: the page itself answered 404). Wikipedia: the terminal "was built in 1889, replacing an earlier one that had been in use since 1864"; "the land on which the extensive yards were built was reclaimed, or filled". Both years documented; the Lehigh Valley terminal on the south side of the Morris Canal basin (opened 1889) is inside the ring. Ring = today's land east of the Turnpike extension from the Morris Canal basin to 330 m north of Morris Pesin Drive.

name: Black Tom: the island, its causeway and the Lehigh Valley fill (Liberty State Park, south end)
note: Standard Oil's National Storage Company built on Black Tom Island in 1876; "by 1880, the island had been transformed into a 25 acre promontory, and a causeway and railroad had been built to connect it with the mainland"; "between 1905 and 1916, the Lehigh Valley Railroad ... expanded the island with landfill". Both years documented. The outline is an estimate: today's land within 330 m of Morris Pesin Drive, which runs along the south end of the park where the causeway and island lay.

name: Port Jersey (the peninsula along Port Jersey Boulevard)
note: "The pier that become Port Jersey was created in the between 1972 and 1976 using landfill." Both years documented. Ring = today's land within 520 m of Port Jersey Boulevard, from 1.1 km east of the line Turnpike extension - Avenue E outward.

name: Military Ocean Terminal at Bayonne (the man-made peninsula along Port Terminal Boulevard)
note: US EPA: "Site use as a port terminal extends back to 1939 when dredged fill material was first used to create the peninsula." Wikipedia: "In 1932, a basic plan was initiated to build a port terminal"; "the Bayonne Naval Drydock base was opened by the Navy in 1942". Both years documented. Ring = today's land east of Avenue E within 420-650 m of Port Terminal Boulevard and of its line carried west to the root of the peninsula.

name: Caven Point: Liberty National golf course, Port Liberte and the Caven Point terminal
note: Port Liberte stands "on Caven Point, formerly one of the last natural sand beaches on the Upper New York Bay"; the park's Caven Point section "is a 22-acre man-made piece of land"; Port Liberte was "commenced in the 1980s" on the older fill. No source at hand dates the terminals' fill (the Army's Caven Point terminal of the First World War and the Lehigh Valley's Claremont Terminal were not verified): estimated bracket. Ring = today's land east of the Turnpike extension between the Black Tom ring and the line of Chapel Avenue.

name: Greenville Yard (Pennsylvania Railroad) and the shore of Greenville
note: "The area, east of the Greenville section of Jersey City was originally tidal marshes and white cedar swamps"; "the yard was first developed in 1904 by the Pennsylvania Railroad". End = the yard; start year estimated. Ring = today's land east of the Turnpike extension and Avenue E between the line of Chapel Avenue and the line of Port Jersey Boulevard.

name: Constable Hook: the refineries' ground and the Bayonne Golf Club landfill
note: Standard Oil's works grew "from its original establishment in 1877"; Standard Oil "bought 176 acres of land on Constable Hook" and was "expanding their refinery" in 1906; Tidewater and Ocean Oil also built there. The Hook itself is natural upland with marsh behind it; no source dates the filling of the marsh and shore: estimated bracket (start = the first refinery). Ring = today's land east of Avenue E within 1.3 km of New Hook Road, plus the golf club outline.

name: Lincoln Park West: land reclaimed from the Hackensack River
note: The Hudson County Parks Commission "began work on the park in 1904"; "by 1925, 85 acre of land had been reclaimed from the Hackensack River in the western portion of the park". Both years documented. Ring = the whole park outline (east and west); only the western, low part is made land.

name: Droyers Point: the city's reclaimed land on Newark Bay (Jersey City Airport, Roosevelt Stadium, Society Hill)
note: "Originally a tidal marsh"; "in the 1920s the land which was owned by the city became the object of development which included land reclamation and the construction of bulkhead"; the Jersey City Airport on it "opened in 1927" and Roosevelt Stadium "opened on April 23, 1937". End = the stadium; start year estimated inside "the 1920s". Ring = the hull of the streets of Society Hill and Droyers Point and of the Gerrity athletic complex + 150 m, on today's land.

name: Kearny Point (South Kearny): Federal Shipbuilding and the industrial fill of the meadow
note: Federal Shipbuilding: "the ship-ways were completed by the fall of 1917 with keels being laid by November 1917". "From the 1920s through the 1960s, more than half the acreage of the Meadowlands lying north of Newark Bay was filled in to make new upland" (Marshall 2004). Start = a year before the ship-ways; end year estimated (estimated bracket for everything but the shipyard). Ring = the Overture outline named Kearny Point.

name: Keegan Landfill, Kearny
note: "NJMC documents indicate that the Keegan landfill began landfill operations in the 1940's, with the majority of landfilling operations taking place in the 1960's. The Keegan Landfill was closed in 1972" (it reopened for construction debris from 2009 and was ordered closed in 2019). Start year estimated inside "the 1940s". Ring = the Overture outline.

name: Malanka Landfill, Secaucus
note: "Size: 66 acres ... Closed to operations in 1983." End documented; start year estimated (no source; illegal and legal dumping in the Meadowlands grew after 1957, Marshall 2004). Ring = the two Overture outlines of that name.

name: Jersey City Reservoir No. 3
note: "It was built between 1871 and 1874 as part of the city's waterworks system"; taken out of service in the 1980s, it still holds water (a lake in a walled park). Start = completion. Ring = the Overture water outline (the water inside the walls, 3.1 ha).

name: Weehawken waterfront: Slough's Meadow, the West Shore Railroad terminal and the Erie yard on Weehawken Cove
note: The strip between the river and the Palisades "has been transformed from an estuary flood zone once called Slough's Meadow to an extensive rail and shipping port"; the West Shore's tunnel under Bergen Hill "had been built in 1881" and its Weehawken Terminal "opened in 1884". Lincoln Harbor stands on "the former Erie Railroad Weehawken Yard, which had partially filled the cove to be built" (not dated: estimated to be of the same years). Ring = Weehawken's land east of the line Willow Avenue - Port Imperial Boulevard.

name: River front under the Palisades: West New York, Guttenberg and North Bergen
note: The railway yards and industry on the narrow shelf north of the West Shore terminal (opened 1884). No source dates this fill: estimated bracket. Ring = today's land east of Port Imperial Boulevard and River Road in the three towns.

name: Edgewater river front (east of River Road)
note: "Early in the 20th century the addition of landfill to the Hudson River changed the borough's appearance"; "in 1922, landfill was dumped into the Hudson River from the construction site of Yankee Stadium in the Bronx, which gives Veteran's Field its current dimensions"; industry "filled 3 mi of the shoreline". Years estimated inside "early in the 20th century" (estimated bracket). Ring = Edgewater's land east of River Road.

name: Meadowlands Sports Complex (East Rutherford)
note: "Ground was broken on Giants Stadium and the Meadowlands Racetrack on November 19, 1972"; "Giants Stadium opened on October 10, 1976" (the racetrack 1 September 1976, the arena 2 July 1981). Both dates documented. Ring = the hull of the stadium, arena, racetrack and mall footprints + 450 m: an estimated outline, it contains marsh that was never filled.

name: Teterboro Airport
note: Walter C. Teter "acquired the property in 1917, and North American Aviation operated a manufacturing plant on the site during World War I. The first flight from the present airport site was made in 1919"; the Port Authority bought the airport on 2 April 1949. The field lies on the Hackensack meadow at 8.4 ft. Start documented; end year estimated (the purchase stands for the runway extensions, which no source at hand dates). Ring = the airport outline.

name: Overpeck County Park: the landfill on Overpeck Creek
note: "During the 1950s, tide gates were installed on the creek that largely cut off the tidal flow"; from 1954 the towns gave the meadow for a county park; the undeveloped areas "were used as dumping sites for garbage"; "the project began in 2003 and the expanded park opened in 2010" on the closed landfill. Both years documented; the progress between them is not. Ring = the hull of the park and golf course outlines; it spans the creek.

name: Kingsland Landfill (Lyndhurst / North Arlington)
note: "Size: 150 acres ... Landfill closed in 1988." End documented; start year estimated (dumping in the Meadowlands grew quickly after 1957, Marshall 2004). Ring = the Overture outline named Kingsland Landfill (136 ha: larger than the 150 acres, it takes in part of the 1-E landfill, which has no date).

name: Avon Landfill (Lyndhurst)
note: "Size: 91 acres ... Closed to operations in 1980." End documented; start year estimated. Ring = the Overture outline.

name: Erie Landfill (North Arlington)
note: "Size: 38 acres ... The Erie Landfill was closed to operations prior to 1970." End = "prior to 1970"; start year estimated. Ring = the Overture outline.

name: Oradell Reservoir
note: "Construction on the Oradell Reservoir began in 1901 by the dredging of a mill pond. The mill pond dam was replaced in 1911 by a low timber-crib dam ... In 1921, a 22 ft high concrete Oradell Reservoir Dam was built ... The reservoir was completed in 1923." Start = completion; a smaller pond stood here from 1901. Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Oradell Reservoir (part 2)
note: "Construction on the Oradell Reservoir began in 1901 by the dredging of a mill pond. The mill pond dam was replaced in 1911 by a low timber-crib dam ... In 1921, a 22 ft high concrete Oradell Reservoir Dam was built ... The reservoir was completed in 1923." Start = completion; a smaller pond stood here from 1901. Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Lake Tappan (Bergen and Rockland counties)
note: "The reservoir was formed in 1967", impounded by the Tappan Dam on the Hackensack River, straddling the state line. Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Woodcliff Lake reservoir
note: The borough was renamed Woodcliff Lake on 1 March 1910, "after the creation of the reservoir". Start year estimated: the article only bounds it (before March 1910); the usual date of about 1903-05 was not verified. Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Port Newark
note: "The city of Newark started constructing Port Newark in 1914, dredging a ship channel one mile long from Newark Bay into the Meadowlands. The city mixed the dredged fill with garbage and ashes and dumped it on the wetlands on the north side of the channel. Additional portions of the Newark Meadows were similarly reclaimed during the 1920s for the expansion of Port Newark" (Marshall 2004). Start documented; end year estimated from "during the 1920s"; the Port Authority (from 1948) extended the port southward (not dated separately). Ring = the Newark part of the Overture outline Port Newark-Elizabeth.

name: Newark Liberty International Airport
note: "The City of Newark started building the airport in 1928 on 68 acre of marshland"; "a land reclamation project to create 68 acre of level ground, 6 ft above sea level"; opened 1 October 1928; the Port Authority took over in 1948 and enlarged it; the Newark Meadows were "totally filled in" between 1914 and 1974 (Marshall 2004). Start documented; end = the end of that bracket; the stages between are not dated. Ring = the airport outline (797 ha).

name: Weequahic Lake
note: The reservation took in "265 acres of saltwater wetland"; "in 1903, a dam was built across the northern end of the lake to arrest the flow of Bound Creek from Newark Bay, causing the water level to rise and creating the depth now seen in the lake". Before 1903 the basin was tidal marsh and creek. Ring = the Overture water outline.

name: Branch Brook Park lake
note: "In 1898, a public appropriation financed the conversion of the swamp into a landscaped lake." Largest water outline inside the park. Ring = the Overture water outline.

name: Orange Reservoir (South Mountain Reservation)
note: "In the 1880s, Orange bought the land and built dams, creating the Orange Reservoir and Campbell's Pond in Millburn." Start year estimated inside "the 1880s". Ring = the Overture water outline.

name: Elizabeth Marine Terminal (Port Elizabeth)
note: "In 1958, the port authority dredged another shipping channel" (the Elizabeth Channel); the first terminal on it was Sea-Land's. "Between 1914 and 1974, the Newark Meadows portion of the Meadowlands was totally filled in and covered by the Port Newark/Elizabeth marine terminal, Newark ... Airport, and the New Jersey Turnpike" (Marshall 2004). Start documented; end = the end of that bracket. Ring = the Elizabeth part of the Overture outline.

name: Lake Surprise (Watchung Reservation)
note: "The lake was created in 1845 for David Felt's papermill." Ring = the Overture water outline.

name: Wanaque Reservoir
note: "The reservoir came into being in 1928 by the construction of the Raymond Dam along the river in Wanaque. After eight years of construction, water was delivered to customers for the first time in 1930." Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Monksville Reservoir
note: "Construction of the reservoir was started in 1985. Building of the actual dam started in March 1987 and was completed in August 1987. The reservoir filled quickly and was full by October 1987." Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Pompton Lake
note: "The lake was formed by the construction of the Pompton Lake Dam in 1908 after a prior wooden dam was destroyed by a flood in 1903": a mill pond stood here before 1903 (not drawn). Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Greenwood Lake (New Jersey and New York): the lake as raised by the dam of 1837
note: "In 1837, the lake was again dammed, but at the location of the current dam, this time by the Morris Canal & Banking Company to supply water to the Pompton Feeder of the Morris Canal." A natural lake (Long Pond), dammed before, lay in the valley: only the margins and the ends were flooded in 1837. The terrain stage must keep water inside this ring before 1837 as well. Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Packanack Lake (Wayne)
note: "A valley of marshland that in 1928 would be cleared of trees and brush; blocked at the south with an earth and clay dam to form Packanack Lake." Ring = the Overture water outline.

name: Charlotteburg Reservoir (Passaic and Morris counties)
note: City of Newark, Department of Water and Sewer Utilities: "In 1957 the City of Newark constructed the Charlotteburg reservoir/dam and the Pequannock Screen Building, located immediately downstream from the reservoir intake." The Pequannock River here is the county line. Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Croton Point: the county landfill on the marsh of the neck
note: "A substantial portion of the land on which the park is situated today was the site of a landfill, which was operated by the Westchester County government from 1927 to 1986. A 1931 map shows the landfill area as marsh." Both years documented. Ring = the whole park outline; the point itself is natural.

name: Sleepy Hollow: the General Motors plant site
note: "The 90 acre plant was in operation, with short interruptions, from 1900 to 1996" on the former Kingsland estate's waterfront. No source at hand dates the filling of the river for the plant: estimated bracket (start = the first factory). Ring = the Overture outline of the redevelopment site + 30 m.

name: Hudson River Railroad: the causeways, the coves cut off and the made land west of the tracks (Yonkers to Croton)
note: The company was "not fully organized until March 4, 1847"; "service began on the first 41 mi of the line from Chambers Street ... to Peekskill on September 29, 1849". The line runs on fill along and across the river's coves. Both dates documented for the railroad; later fill west of the tracks (Yonkers, Hastings, Dobbs Ferry, Irvington, Tarrytown, Ossining) is inside the ring and not dated. Ring = today's land west of the westernmost track of the Hudson Line (Overture rail, sampled every 120 m of northing) and 45 m east of it, from the Yonkers line to Croton Point; natural points are inside.

name: Playland, Rye
note: "Construction commenced in September 1927, and was completed in six months"; "built in 1928, the 280 acre park". The park was laid out on the shore and marsh of Manursing; how much of it is made land is not stated (estimated outline). Ring = the hull of the amusement park and Playland Lake + 120 m, on today's land.

name: Glen Island, New Rochelle: five islands joined
note: "Although now one island, the site originally consisted of one large main island in close proximity to at least four smaller nearby islands, a number of rocky outcroppings, low-lying flats, and salt marshes"; John H. Starin made it a resort from 1879. Start = Starin; end year estimated (Westchester County made it a park in the 1920s). Ring = the island outline.

name: New Croton Reservoir
note: "Construction on a New Croton Dam began in 1892"; "in 1906, the New Croton Dam was completed, expanding the existing impoundment into the New Croton Reservoir". Croton Lake, behind the Old Croton Dam of 1842 ("built ... between 1837 and 1842"; "submerged to a depth of 34 ft" in 1906), filled the upper part of this outline from 1842: its outline is not on disk and is not drawn. Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Kensico Reservoir / Rye Lake
note: "In 1885, the old Kensico Dam was built"; "the construction of the new dam began in 1913 and was concluded in 1917". Start = the new dam, which made today's outline; the smaller reservoir of 1885 behind the old dam is not drawn. Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Titicus Reservoir
note: "It has been supplying the system since 1893." Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Muscoot Reservoir
note: "The reservoir was constructed at the beginning of the 20th century, and was completed in 1905." Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Amawalk Reservoir
note: "Formed by impounding the middle of the Muscoot River ... and put into service in 1897." Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Cross River Reservoir
note: "The reservoir was finally put into service in 1908." Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Grassy Sprain Reservoir
note: "It was completed in 1876 by the City of Yonkers as the city's main storage reservoir." Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Hillview Reservoir
note: "It was built within a six-year period from 1909-1915 by the New York City Board of Water Supply to receive water from the newly constructed Catskill Aqueduct." A basin on a hilltop, not a flooded valley. Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Tarrytown Reservoir
note: "The reservoir was completed in 1897 by the village of Tarrytown"; decommissioned in 1993, it still holds water. Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Long Beach: the barrier island raised and bulkheaded for the resort
note: William H. Reynolds "acquired the oceanfront from private owners and the rest of the island from the Town of Hempstead in 1907; he planned to build a boardwalk, homes, and hotels"; "dredges created a channel 1000 ft wide on the north side of the island" (Reynolds Channel); "the community became an incorporated village in 1913". Start documented; end year estimated (the incorporation stands for the end of the dredging; the article does not say where the dredged sand went). Ring = the municipal outline of Long Beach on today's land; the natural beach ridge is inside.

name: Atlantic Beach
note: "In 1923, the village's first developer, Atlantic Beach Associates", began; in 1926 Austin and Talbot "completed Pettit's preliminary dredging and shoring work, and proceeded to subdivide the property"; the bridge "was opened and dedicated on June 29, 1927". Both years documented. Ring = the municipal outline of Atlantic Beach on today's land; the natural beach ridge is inside.

name: Island Park (Barnum Island)
note: The island was sold to developers in 1909 and 1911: "minimal development at that time included construction of several canals, before work was abandoned. New developers bought the island in 1921, and started building ... starting in 1922." Start documented; end year estimated. Ring = the municipal outline of Island Park on today's land; the natural beach ridge is inside.

name: Jones Beach State Park: the island raised with dredged sand
note: "When Moses' group first surveyed Jones Island in the 1920s, it was swampy and only 2 ft above sea level"; "huge dredgers brought sand from the bay bottom, eventually raising the island to 12 ft above sea level"; "in the summer of 1928, thousands of men worked on the beach planting the grass by hand"; "the park opened to the public on August 4, 1929, along with the causeway". End documented; start year estimated. Ring = the park outline on today's land.

name: Hempstead Lake (the Brooklyn water works' storage reservoir)
note: The lake was "first proposed in 1870 to supply water to Brooklyn"; "the Mill River ... was dammed to form the 167-acre reservoir"; in 1947 a dam for the Southern State Parkway cut off its northern third. Start year estimated: the article gives no completion year (1873 is the usual one and was not verified). Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Lake DeForest
note: "A reservoir in Clarkstown, New York, created in 1956 by impounding the Hackensack River"; dedicated 13 March 1957. Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Lake Sebago (Harriman State Park)
note: "The lake was created in 1925 by the Palisades Interstate Park Commission." Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Lake Welch (Harriman State Park)
note: "By 1942, the lake was completed using workers from the Civilian Conservation Corps"; it drowned the hamlet of Sandyfield. Ring = the Overture water outlines, joined across causeways by a 30 m closing.

name: Piermont: the Erie Railroad pier
note: "The railroad built a long pier into the river near the creek in 1839 as its principal terminal." End documented; start year estimated (a year of work). Ring = the largest piece of the village's land east of Piermont Avenue: the mile-long pier with the made ground at its root.
